start.title: Hundreds of Accounts Hijacked in One Night
start.bestWhy: Stop the abnormal login attempts and log out the compromised accounts first, then find the root cause from evidence.
start.text: You run a student chat app with 1,000 users. This morning a flood of reports comes in: "Someone got into our account and sent scam links to all our friends." You find that last night there were 50,000 login attempts in a single hour. Most failed, but 300 accounts were successfully accessed. What do you do first?
start.source: NIST SP 800-61 (incident response); Have I Been Pwned (passwords leaked from other sites)

choices.label: Temporarily rate-limit logins, force all 300 compromised accounts to log out on all devices, remove the scam links, then investigate what happened.
choices.out: The app slows down for about 6 hours and some users have trouble logging in — but the credential stuffing stops, the compromised accounts are cut off, and you now have time to read the logs.
u: Login difficulties for 6 hours — some users don't stick around.
choices.lesson: Contain first: stop the ongoing attack and cut the attacker out of compromised accounts, then find the root cause from evidence.

choices.label: Delete all the scam messages and let the app keep running.
choices.out: The day looks quiet, but you still don't know how the attacker got in — and they're still logged in to those 300 accounts.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Removing the results is not the same as fixing the root cause. If the entry point is still open, the attacker will just do it again.

choices.label: Move the app to a new server — you think someone hacked into the server.
choices.out: The migration takes a full day and users can't access the app — but the logs you read later show no one hacked the server. The attacker simply logged in with valid credentials.
u: Server migration — some users drop off.
choices.lesson: Base your hypothesis on evidence, not gut feeling. Fixing the wrong thing wastes time while the attack is still ongoing.

choices.label: Shut down the app and rewrite the entire login system and app from scratch.
choices.out: You shut the app down for two weeks to rewrite it. Many users move to other apps while waiting, but the new system won't have the same vulnerability.
u: App down for two weeks — users move to other apps.
choices.lesson: A full rewrite looks safe but is costly and risky — code written in a rush tends to introduce new vulnerabilities.

investigate.title: Where Did the Passwords Come From?
investigate.bestWhy: There are two root causes — both must be closed: protect against login brute-forcing, and store passwords securely.
investigate.text: From the logs you find that the attacker didn't hack the system — they used a list of emails and passwords leaked from other websites and tried them against your app one by one (credential stuffing). Users who reused passwords across sites got compromised. And while investigating, you find something even more alarming: your database stores every user's password in plain, readable text. There are two root causes: (1) no login rate limiting and no 2-step authentication, and (2) passwords are stored without hashing. How do you fix this?
investigate.source: NIST SP 800-63B (rate limiting, blocking known-leaked passwords, hashed storage); OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet

choices.label: Rate-limit login attempts, enable 2-step, block known-leaked passwords, and convert all stored passwords to hashed form — then require everyone to set a new password.
choices.out: You spend one day fixing both issues. Users set new passwords and many enable 2-step. You then fire known-leaked credentials at the app yourself — all of them are blocked.
u: Users must set new passwords.
choices.lesson: Two key principles: prevent mass login attempts, and never store passwords in readable form — use hashing so that even you can't read them.

choices.label: Rate-limit logins first — deal with password storage later.
choices.out: The credential stuffing stops and the app is back up quickly — but everyone's password is still stored as plain text in the database.
u: Brief app downtime.
choices.lesson: A half-fix creates a false sense of security. If the database ever leaks, every password goes with it instantly.

choices.label: Convert passwords to hashed form first — leave login rate limiting for later because you're worried users will complain it's inconvenient.
choices.out: The stored passwords are now safe — but the attacker can still try unlimited leaked credentials from other sites against your app.
u: Brief app downtime.
choices.lesson: Worrying that users will complain shouldn't be a reason to leave a vulnerability open. Login rate limiting barely affects normal users.

partialClient.title: Accounts Hijacked Again
partialClient.bestWhy: Login rate limiting must happen at the Server. Client-side checks can always be bypassed by a bot.
partialClient.text: Five days later, the attacker returns with a fresh batch of leaked credentials and fires 80,000 more login attempts. Another 150 accounts are compromised, and the attacker sends scam shop links to every victim's friends. Several users have already transferred money.

u: More accounts hijacked — friends tricked into transferring money.

partialClient.source: NIST SP 800-63B (server-side rate limiting); CISA Secure Our World (2-step)

choices.label: Rate-limit logins at the Server, enable 2-step, log out the compromised accounts, and notify affected users to change their passwords everywhere they reused them.
choices.out: You close every entry point. Firing known-leaked credentials at the app yourself — all blocked. And affected users have changed their passwords on other sites too.
u: App taken down to apply the fix.
choices.lesson: Rate limiting and 2-step make passwords leaked from other sites useless against your app. And remind users: never reuse passwords across sites.

choices.label: Add client-side code in the app to allow only 5 wrong login attempts.
choices.out: In the app it looks like it works — but bots don't use your app. They send login requests directly to the system and bypass the counter within the hour.
u: Bot bypasses the in-app check successfully.
choices.lesson: Client-side checks (checks inside the app) improve the user experience but are not security — attackers have full control over their own client.

partialRules.title: Database Leaked
partialRules.bestWhy: Fix everything completely, check what data was exposed, and notify users so they can change their passwords everywhere they reused them.
partialRules.text: Five days later, someone discovers that a backup of your app's database was accidentally left as a public link. The file contains the emails, birthdays, student IDs, and passwords of all 1,000 users in plain readable text — and someone has already posted it to a hacker forum.

u: Users who hear the news — some stop using the app.

partialRules.source: EU GDPR Articles 5 (data minimization) and 33–34 (breach notification); OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet

choices.label: Remove the public link, hash all stored passwords, require everyone to set a new password, stop storing unnecessary data like birthdays, and notify all users directly — telling them to change their passwords on every other site they reused them.
choices.out: You message every user explaining what was exposed and what to do. Some are angry, but many thank you for telling them quickly — and they make it in time to change their passwords elsewhere.
u: Some users leave after being notified.
choices.lesson: Collect only what you need — data you don't store can't leak. And notifying users quickly lets them protect themselves. (International data protection law such as the EU's GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority within 72 hours and notifying affected individuals when the risk is high.)

choices.label: Quietly remove the public link and don't announce it — no one has asked about it yet.
choices.out: The app returns to normal, but users who reuse that password for social media and email don't know, so they don't change it.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Staying silent doesn't make the leaked data disappear — it just leaves users unable to protect themselves, and the truth will come out.

choices.label: Take the app down and bring in an external expert to audit the entire system before making any announcement.
choices.out: The expert finds two more publicly exposed backup files and confirms exactly what was leaked. You announce with a clear remediation plan, but the app has to stay down for a long time.
u: Extended downtime — some users don't wait.
choices.lesson: External experts are worth it when you're unsure of the damage scope — but you need to weigh that against the time your service has to stay down.

repeat.title: Hit Again
repeat.bestWhy: Being hit again means the root cause is still there. Stop, fix everything properly, and communicate honestly.
repeat.text: A few days later, hundreds more accounts are hijacked, scam links flood the app, and someone finds your users' passwords posted on a hacker forum. The original entry point is still open and data is already out. What do you do?
repeat.source: NIST SP 800-61 (incident response); EU GDPR Article 34

choices.label: Temporarily shut down the app, rate-limit logins, enable 2-step, hash all passwords, then communicate openly about what happened.
choices.out: You fix both issues completely, require everyone to set a new password, and announce the situation honestly. Users are upset, but most see that you're taking responsibility.
u: App down — some users lost from the news.
choices.lesson: Being hit again means the first round didn't fix the root cause. Stop, review the evidence, fix everything completely, and communicate straightforwardly.

choices.label: Fix the system completely but don't tell users — you don't want to alarm them.
choices.out: The system is genuinely more secure — but users whose passwords leaked don't know, and are still using the same password on social media and email.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Concealing an incident doesn't protect users — it only delays the day the truth comes out.

choices.label: Give out free stickers and premium features to win users back — fix the system later.
choices.out: New users sign up immediately, but the attacker can see the entry point is still open and hijacks new accounts every day.
u: Free rewards bring some users back.
choices.lesson: Polishing your image without fixing the system just delays the problem — and it comes back harder.

rewrite.title: New App, New Holes
rewrite.tag: New Vulnerabilities from a Rushed Build
rewrite.bestWhy: Close all holes before going live: encrypt connections and protect the admin account with multiple layers.
rewrite.text: Two weeks later the new version of the app launches. It has login rate limiting, 2-step for users, and hashed password storage. Some users return following the news. But in the rush, you forgot two things: (1) the new web login page doesn't use HTTPS (no padlock icon), so passwords are sent in readable form over public Wi-Fi; and (2) the admin panel still uses the default password. A bot is now trying to guess the admin password about 3,000 times per hour.

u: Some users return following the relaunch news.

rewrite.source: Google Safety Center (HTTPS and the padlock icon); CISA Secure by Design (no default passwords)

choices.label: Enable HTTPS on all pages, change the admin default password, enable 2-step for the admin account, and rate-limit admin login attempts.
choices.out: All connections are now encrypted. The bot keeps trying but gets blocked after a few failed attempts — and even if it guesses the password right, it can't get in without the code from your phone.
u: Users feel confident as the app stays stable.
choices.lesson: HTTPS encrypts data in transit so no one on the same Wi-Fi can read it. Admin accounts should also be protected with multiple layers (defence in depth).

choices.label: Enable HTTPS and change the admin password to a longer one.
choices.out: Passwords are no longer readable in transit, and the admin password is longer — but the bot can still try an unlimited number of times, and there's no second factor if the password is phished.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: A strong password is a good first layer — but it shouldn't be the only layer.

choices.label: Don't do it right now — need to promote the new version first.
choices.out: First-day user numbers are great — but that night the bot successfully guesses the admin password.
u: Promotional campaign pays off.
choices.lesson: A risk that hasn't materialized yet is not a risk that doesn't exist. A bot actively guessing passwords is clear evidence the app is already being targeted.

wave2.title: A Fake Login Page for Your App
wave2.bestWhy: Warn users immediately, report the fake page for takedown, and give key accounts a second factor.
wave2.text: About a week passes. The previous holes are closed, but the attacker changes tactics. A post circulates on social media: "Get free premium features — just log in through this link." The link leads to a fake login page that looks exactly like your app. One of your moderators has already shared the link.
wave2.source: CISA Secure Our World: Recognize and Report Phishing; UK NCSC: Phishing attacks

choices.label: Immediately alert users inside the app, report the fake page to the hosting provider for takedown, and enable 2-step for every team account.
choices.out: The fake page is taken down within the day. Most users see the warning before clicking, and even if a team member entered their password on the fake page, the second factor blocks the attacker.
u: App stable — users return.
choices.lesson: Free stuff + a link + a login page is the classic phishing signal. Always log in through the app or by typing the address yourself. 2-step protects you even if your password is stolen.

choices.label: Do nothing — it's not our website.
choices.out: Multiple users and moderators enter their passwords on the fake page. A few hours later someone logs into team accounts using those credentials.
u: No visible effect yet.
choices.lesson: A fake page using your app's name is your problem — because your users and your team are the targets.

choices.label: Post a warning on the app's official page only.
choices.out: Some users see the warning, but the fake page is still up, and team accounts still have no second factor.
u: No additional incidents.
choices.lesson: Warning helps, but you should also report the fake page for takedown and add a second factor — so that anyone who misses the warning doesn't bring down the whole system.

takeover.title: Team Account Hijacked
takeover.bestWhy: You need to cut the attacker off from every access point — not just change the password. Then audit what they did.
takeover.text: The attacker is inside the app's backend using a legitimate team account. They sent scam messages from the app's official account to every user, banned dozens of real users, and viewed user data — all without exploiting a single line of code.

u: Scam messages from the official account — many users lost.

takeover.source: NIST SP 800-61 (incident response); OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet

choices.label: Log out every active session on all devices, change passwords on all team accounts, enable 2-step, audit the logs for what was done, reverse all bans, and notify users.
choices.out: You go through every change one by one, lift all bans, delete the scam messages, close every access point, and notify users directly.
u: App down for remediation — some users leave after being notified.
choices.lesson: When an account is hijacked, you must cut the attacker off from every access point — active sessions, tokens, and keys — not just change the password. Then audit everything they did.

choices.label: Change the password only, then reopen the app.
choices.out: The attacker is still logged in on their device. They come back the next night and send another round of scam messages.
u: Brief downtime to change the password.
Attacker returns via the still-active session.
choices.lesson: Changing the password alone isn't enough. If the attacker still has an active session, they can keep coming back. You must log them out of every device.

choices.label: Hire an external security team to audit the entire backend, then follow their recommendations.
choices.out: The team discovers the attacker created a hidden team account. They remove it, set up 2-step, and users are notified. Costly, but thorough.
u: Extended downtime and audit fees — some users don't wait.
choices.lesson: Attackers often leave a "backdoor" behind. Expert eyes can find things you'd miss — but it comes at a cost in time and money.

news.title: The Story Breaks on Social Media
news.bestWhy: If you missed the disclosure window, admit it and act as soon as you realize. The longer you stay silent, the more trust you lose.
news.text: A student posts that their social media account was hacked, and they traced the leaked password back to your app — which they found posted on a hacker forum. The post is shared thousands of times overnight and people start asking whether the app knew about this.

u: News breaks that the app covered up the incident.

news.source: EU GDPR Article 34 (notification of affected individuals); Have I Been Pwned

choices.label: Issue a public statement acknowledging what happened, what data was exposed, what has been fixed, and recommend that everyone change their password on every site where they reused it.
choices.out: You admit you knew earlier and didn't notify anyone. The criticism is heavy — but the clear information helps users protect their other accounts in time, and some still stay.
u: Some users leave after learning they were kept in the dark.
choices.lesson: If you missed the disclosure, fix it the moment you realize. Late transparency is still better than none.

choices.label: Say the data didn't come from our app.
choices.out: Multiple users cross-reference the data and find it matches only what they used in your app. The denial gets shared as a textbook example of an irresponsible app.
u: Caught denying verifiable facts.
choices.lesson: Denying verifiable facts turns a data incident into a full-blown credibility crisis.

choices.label: Take the app down for three days to investigate before issuing any statement.
choices.out: You confirm the full scope of the damage before speaking — but during those three silent days, the rumours travel further, and many users get other accounts hacked in the meantime.
u: Three days of silence — rumours spread.
choices.lesson: Verifying before speaking is good — but if you go silent too long, rumours will tell the story for you.

wave2_blocked.title: Phishing That Failed
wave2_blocked.text: The following week, a fake login page for your app circulates on social media. One moderator already entered their password on the fake page — but the attacker can't get into the account, because every team account has 2-step enabled. You receive an alert about a login attempt from an unknown device.

u: Users see the app running smoothly — no incidents.

wave2_blocked.source: Microsoft Security: MFA blocks nearly all automated account takeovers

choices.label: View summary
choices.out: You change that moderator's password, report the fake page for takedown, and remind the team to stay alert. No damage is done.
u: No damage.
choices.lesson: A second factor means one person's mistake doesn't become a disaster for the whole app.

root.title: A Trustworthy App Builder
root.desc: You stopped credential stuffing, stored passwords securely, layered your defences, and the app still has nearly as many users as before.

rebuilder.title: The Architect Who Started Over
rebuilder.desc: You took the most expensive path — a full rewrite — and still caught the new vulnerabilities that came with the rush. The app is secure, but the user base is not the same.

honest.title: Honest but Bruised
honest.desc: The app took a serious hit, but you told users the truth. The trust that remains is the foundation for a comeback.

survivor.title: A Survivor Who Learned
survivor.desc: The app is still running and the critical holes are closed — even if there were costs along the way.

nomfa.title: Strong on Fixes, Forgot the Second Layer
nomfa.desc: The login system and password storage are fixed, but team accounts still rely on a password alone. The remaining risk is a human one.

cover.title: Covered It Up and Lost the Trust
cover.desc: The system may have been fixed — but not telling users let them get other accounts hacked, and the damage came back harder.

scarred.title: Deep Wounds, Still Standing
scarred.desc: User data took serious damage. The app is still alive, but rebuilding user trust will take a long time.

bleeding.title: Bleeding Out
bleeding.desc: You attracted users with free rewards instead of fixing the system. The attacker hijacks new accounts every day. The app is slowly collapsing with no end to the incident in sight.

collapse.title: The App Had to Shut Down
collapse.desc: The user count dropped too low for the app to survive. Look back and see which decision caused the biggest drop.

AXES.dL: You tend to keep the app running first, even when risk remains.
AXES.dR: You're willing to lose users in the short term to secure the system first.
AXES.dM: You strike a reasonable balance between security and keeping the app running.

AXES.dL: You prefer to verify before acting. The upside is precision; the downside is speed.
AXES.dR: You decide quickly. The upside is stopping incidents fast; the downside is missing things.
AXES.dM: You adjust your pace well to the demands of each situation.

AXES.dL: You tend to prioritize image — which often erodes user trust later.
AXES.dR: You tell users the truth, even when it stings in the short term.
AXES.dM: You haven't faced many situations that forced a clear communication choice yet.

AXES.dL: You tend to choose the fast fix, which sometimes leaves the root cause untouched.
AXES.dR: You think about root causes and long-term consequences.
AXES.dM: You mix quick patches with root-cause fixes.
